words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our science group grew one microbe on a jelly plate.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part of microbe tells you it is too small to see?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The micro part. It means small, so a microbe is a tiny living thing.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our school captains used diplomacy to settle the yard argument.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: What does the -acy ending do to the word diplomat?
words_to_spell_review.answer: It turns it into a state or a skill. Diplomacy is settling things without a fight.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The science teacher warned us that the powder was explosive.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: What does the -ive ending tell you about the powder?
words_to_spell_review.answer: It describes what the powder is like. Explosive means it can blow up.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our mural will depict the wetland behind the school oval.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part of depict means paint?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The pict part. To depict something is to paint it or show it.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Dad heated the soup in the microwave before training.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Why is a microwave called that?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Micro means small. It cooks with very small, very fast waves.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: One laptop had a malfunction during the maths test.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part of malfunction tells you something went wrong?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The mal- prefix. It means bad or wrong, so the laptop worked badly.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The museum gave us a pictorial guide to the goldfields.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: What does a pictorial guide use to explain things?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Pictures. Pict means paint and -al means relating to.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Each photo we took on camp was almost one megabyte.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: How big is a megabyte?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Mega- means million, so a megabyte is about a million bytes.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: We drew a pictograph to show our class lunch orders.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which two parts build pictograph?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Pict means picture and graph means write or record, so it records with pictures.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The pond water held microscopic life we could not see.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: What does microscopic tell you about the life in that water?
words_to_spell_review.answer: It is far too small for your eyes. Micro means small.

words_to_read_new.meaning: eco means house + system means parts that work together: the natural house where every part works together
eco means house + -ology means the study of: the study of the natural house living things share
eco means house + -ology means the study of + -ist means person who: the person who studies the natural house
eco means house + -ology means the study of + -ical means relating to: relating to the study of the natural house
eco means house + -cide means killing: the killing of a whole natural house
eco means house + nom means managing + -ic means having the nature of: having the nature of managing the house
eco means house + nom means managing + -ical means relating to: relating to managing the house so nothing is wasted
eco means house + nom means managing + -ist means person who: the person who studies how a country manages its house
eco means house + nom means managing + -ise means to make: to make the house run on less

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Learn eco once and you can read and spell a whole family of environment words you have never met."
READ each word as it appears, then connect eco to the card meaning: house.
ecosystem - eco means house + system means parts that work together: the natural house where every living part works together.
ecology - eco means house + -ology means the study of: the study of the natural house living things share.
ecologist - eco means house + -ology means the study of + -ist means person who: the person who studies the natural house.
ecological - eco means house + -ology means the study of + -ical means relating to: relating to the study of the natural house.
ecocide - eco means house + -cide means killing: the killing of a whole natural house.
economic - eco means house + nom means managing + -ic means having the nature of: having the nature of managing the house, and a country is one very big house.
economical - eco means house + nom means managing + -ical means relating to: relating to managing the house so well that nothing is wasted.
economist - eco means house + nom means managing + -ist means person who: the person who studies how a country manages its house.
economise - eco means house + nom means managing + -ise means to make: to make the house run on less.
Memory hook: eco is a house with no walls - a pond, a paddock, a reef is an address living things share. Challenge: list five living things at one eco address in our school yard by Friday.

items: 1. house + study of + person = ?    2. house + killing = ?

review.notes:
Why learned: ei says long i here, not the usual /ee/, because the seis part came straight from Greek.
Say it: SIZE-muh-graf, three beats. Tap them, then write seis - mo - graph.
Quick link: graph means write or record, the same graph as pictograph, so only the seis part is unfair.

Why learned: the ou says a plain /uh/ and the French -age ending says /ahzh/, not the /ij/ of village.
Say it: KAM-uh-flahzh, three beats. Write cam - ou - flage in three chunks.
Quick link: the colours and patterns that hide an animal inside its own ecosystem.

new.notes:
Why learned: the ci says /sh/, which c and i almost never do together, and the final es says /eez/.
Say it: SPEE-sheez, two beats. Say spee, then sheez, and write spe - cies in two chunks.
Link: a species is one kind of living thing, so an ecosystem is built out of the species inside it.
You will write this word in every science report about living things this term.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Name the appositive and teach the cover test that finds it.
WHY THIS WEEK: students write two short sentences where one would do, so the reader loses the thread.
PREP: OG books open before the I do. All grammar this week is written in the OG book.

i_do.title: What is an appositive?
i_do.rule: An appositive renames the noun beside it, inside two commas.
i_do.example:
Mia, our team captain, scored first.
our team captain = renames Mia
items: A noun is a naming word: Mia, captain, pond, teacher.
Test: cover the extra words and read it again.
i_do.routine: Eyes on me - watch the commas
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: where do the commas go?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: our team captain renames Mia.
1. SAY: "An appositive is a few extra words that rename the noun beside them, so you can tell your reader who someone is without stopping to write a second sentence."
2. MODEL: point at Mia. SAY: "Mia is the naming word. Straight after it, our team captain says who Mia is."
3. MODEL: cover the extra words. SAY: "Mia scored first still works, so those words are extra - that is why commas hold them in."
4. ASK: "What job do the two commas do?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: they hold the extra words in.
TRAP: thinking the appositive is the person doing the action. Fix: cover it, read the sentence, then name the noun again.
---
Purpose: day one names the appositive and models the cover test. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]

we_do.title: Find the appositive
we_do.rule: An appositive renames the noun beside it, inside two commas.
we_do.example: Our dog, a noisy kelpie, waits at the gate.
items: Write the words that rename Our dog.
Prove it: cover them and read the sentence again.
we_do.routine: OG books - write it - pens down
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: a noisy kelpie renames Our dog.
1. SAY: "Write the words that rename Our dog. Just those words, nothing else."
2. TIME: 20 seconds in your OG book, then pens down and books up.
3. SCAN the back row's books first. 80%+ -> take the reason. Less -> cover the words together, re-read, then re-ask.
4. ASK: "How do you know a noisy kelpie is the appositive?" 5 sec, cold call two students. EXPECT: it renames Our dog and the sentence still works without it.
TRAP: writing the whole sentence out. Fix: point at the two commas, take only what sits between them, student rewrites it.
---
Purpose: guided use of the cover test on one clear model. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]

you_do.title: Appositive - your turn
you_do.rule: Your turn: write the appositive from each sentence.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
Sam, my little brother, lost a boot.
Appositive: my little brother
items: A) Rosa, our captain, cheered loudly.
B) Our ute, a rusty truck, stalled.
you_do.footer: Check: does it say who or what?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - our captain. B - a rusty truck.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then write just the appositive for A and for B."
2. TIME: 90 seconds in your OG book. Work on your own.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "read only the words between the two commas - do they say WHO Rosa is?" Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> cover B's extra words together, then re-check.
TRAP: including the noun itself. Fix: point at the first comma, start after it, student rewrites the answer.
EXTENSION: Write one sentence about our class with an appositive, then rewrite it as two separate sentences and say which version a reader prefers.
HELP: Give the two answers our captain and a rusty truck; students match each to A or B first.
---
Purpose: independent use of the cover test; tomorrow punctuates it. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) Rosa, our captain, cheered loudly. Appositive: our captain
B) Our ute, a rusty truck, stalled. Appositive: a rusty truck
EXTENSION: e.g. Ari, our class gardener, waters the beds. Two sentences: Ari waters the beds. Ari is our class gardener. The appositive version is shorter and keeps the flow.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - Appositive
you_do.check_rule: Tick each correct appositive. Fix any that does not match.
check_items: A) Rosa, our captain, cheered loudly. = our captain
Cover it and Rosa cheered loudly still works.
B) Our ute, a rusty truck, stalled. = a rusty truck
Cover it and Our ute stalled still works.
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: say who they are.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A - our captain. B - a rusty truck.
1. MODEL: "In A I cover our captain. Rosa cheered loudly still works, so those words are the appositive."
2. SAY: "Now tick each answer that matches. Fix any answer that is different."
3. ASK: "Why do the commas have to come in a pair?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: one opens the extra words and one closes them.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> cover B together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "When you edit your next draft, find a name your reader might not know and add commas with a few words that say who they are."
TRAP: ticking an answer that keeps the noun in. Fix: read from after the first comma, then correct it.

Purpose: the answer slide shows how the cover test decides each one. [You Do | Feedback | Grammar | HITS 5]

words_to_spell_review.prompt: How big is a nodule?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Small. The -ule ending means small, so a nodule is a small lump.

words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ology ending. Eco means house, so ecology studies the natural home.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: My little sister is sensitive to loud noise at assembly.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: What does the -ive ending tell you about my sister?
words_to_spell_review.answer: It describes what she is like. She feels loud noise very strongly.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The mural depicted our creek before the town was built.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The wind left the sports shed in complete disorder.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part of disorder tells you the order has come apart?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The dis- prefix. It means apart, so the order has been pulled apart.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The lab report showed microbial growth in the fish tank.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: An economist came to explain how shop prices are set.

words_to_spell_review.prompt: What does voracious tell you about the chicks?

words_to_read_new.meaning: carn means flesh + vore means eating: an animal that eats flesh
carn means flesh + vore means eating + -ous means full of: describes a meat eater
carn means flesh + -age means the result of: the result left when flesh is torn
carn means flesh + val means farewell: the old farewell to meat, now a street party
carn means flesh + -ation means the state of: the flower named for its flesh-pink colour
carn means flesh + -ian names the kind: a stone the colour of flesh
in- means into + carn means flesh + -ate means to make: made into flesh
in- means into + carn means flesh + -ation means the state of: the state of being made into flesh
re- means again + in- means into + carn means flesh + -ate means to make: to be made into flesh again

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Learn carn once and every meat word in science, history and even the garden opens up for you."
READ each word as it appears, then connect carn to the card meaning: flesh, meat.
carnivore - carn means flesh + vore means eating: an animal that eats flesh. You met vore on Friday - here is the other half.
carnivorous - carn means flesh + vore means eating + -ous means full of: full of flesh-eating habits, so it describes a meat eater.
carnage - carn means flesh + -age means the result of: the result left when flesh is torn, so a scene of terrible destruction.
carnival - carn means flesh + val means farewell: the old farewell to meat before a season without it, and now a street party.
carnation - carn means flesh + -ation means the state of: the flower named for its flesh-pink colour.
carnelian - carn means flesh + -ian names the kind: a stone the colour of flesh, a deep orange red.
incarnate - in- means into + carn means flesh + -ate means to make: made into flesh, given a body you can see.
incarnation - in- means into + carn means flesh + -ation means the state of: the state of being made into flesh, one life in one body.
reincarnate - re- means again + in- means into + carn means flesh + -ate means to make: to be made into flesh again in a new body.
Memory hook: carn is the butcher's window - if carn is in the word, picture meat or the pink of flesh. Challenge: find one carn word on a menu, one in a garden and one in a museum by Friday.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Punctuate the appositive - one comma opens it and one comma closes it.
WHY THIS WEEK: a missing comma makes the reader stumble and reread.
PREP: OG books open. All grammar this week is written in the OG book.

i_do.title: Two commas, one job
i_do.rule: An appositive renames the noun beside it, inside two commas.
i_do.example:
Our teacher, Mr Lee, marked the books.
one comma opens, one comma closes
items: Cover Mr Lee - Our teacher marked the books still works.
Miss one comma and the reader trips over the sentence.
i_do.footer: Stem: The commas go before and after ...
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: the commas go before and after Mr Lee.
1. SAY: "An appositive renames the noun beside it, and it needs a pair of commas so your reader knows exactly where the extra words start and stop."
2. MODEL: point at the first comma. SAY: "This one opens the extra words. Mr Lee tells us who our teacher is."
3. MODEL: point at the second comma. SAY: "This one closes them, and the sentence carries on: marked the books."

words_to_read_new.meaning: join is the root on its own: to put two things together
joint is the root with a t on the end: the place where two parts join
joint means the place where two join + -ly means in that way: done by two together
junct means join + -tion means the act of: the place where two roads join
junct means join + -ure means the state of: the point where two moments join
con- means together + join means join: to join two things into one
con- means together + junct means join + -tion means the act of: the word that joins two parts of a sentence
con- means together + junct means join + -ive means relating to: relating to joining two things
en- means on + join means join: to join an order onto someone
in- means onto + junct means join + -tion means the act of: a court order joined onto you to make you stop
dis- means apart + joint means the place where two join + -ed means past tense: pulled apart at the joins
re- means back + join means join + -der names the thing: the reply you join straight back on

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Learn junct once and roads, bones, sentences and court orders all start using the same word part."
READ each word as it appears, then connect junct to the card meaning: join.
join - join is the root on its own: to put two things together.
joint - joint is the root with a t on the end: the place where two parts join, like your knee.
jointly - joint means the place where two join + -ly means in that way: done by two people together.
junction - junct means join + -tion means the act of: the place where two roads join.
juncture - junct means join + -ure means the state of: the point where two moments join, the moment that decides what happens next.
conjoin - con- means together + join means join: to join two things into one.
conjunction - con- means together + junct means join + -tion means the act of: the word that joins two parts of a sentence together.
conjunctive - con- means together + junct means join + -ive means relating to: relating to joining two things together.
enjoin - en- means on + join means join: to join an order onto someone, telling them they must do it.
injunction - in- means onto + junct means join + -tion means the act of: a court order joined onto you to make you stop.
disjointed - dis- means apart + joint means the place where two join + -ed means past tense: pulled apart at the joins, so nothing flows.
rejoinder - re- means back + join means join + -der names the thing: the reply you join straight back onto what someone said.
Memory hook: junct is the T-intersection - two roads, two bones, two clauses meeting at one point. Challenge: count three junctions on the walk home and name what joins at each one.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "When you finish, turn one spelling word into a question you could ask a partner."
2. CHECK: the question must show the join meaning, not just use the word.
EXTENSION: Build a new word from join or joint with one taught ending, then write its full morpheme sum and meaning.
Then use your new word in one sentence about a road or about your knee.

My uncle a truck driver waved.
I wrote it with no commas. Fix me.
items: Where do the two commas go? Show me with fingers.
Then read it back the right way.
we_do.footer: Stem: The commas go after ... and after ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: after uncle and after driver - My uncle, a truck driver, waved.
1. SAY: "I have written this with no commas at all. Catch me out."
2. TIME: 15 seconds thinking, voices off, then fingers up on three.
3. SCAN every hand. 80%+ -> read it back correctly together. Less -> read my version aloud so they hear it run on, then re-ask.
4. ASK: "How do you know a truck driver is the part inside the commas?" 5 sec, cold call two students. EXPECT: it renames uncle and the sentence works without it.
TRAP: putting one comma after waved. Fix: read to the end of the naming words, hear the stop, move the comma.
---

you_do.title: Exit ticket - the appositive
you_do.rule: Your turn: copy each sentence and add the two commas.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
Our cat Tiger sleeps all day.
Our cat, Tiger, sleeps all day.
items: A) The kelpie Bluey rounded up the sheep.
B) Our principal Ms Okafor opened the fair.
you_do.footer: Check: did you write both commas?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - commas around Bluey. B - commas around Ms Okafor.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then copy A and B and put both commas in."
2. TIME: 90 seconds in your OG book, then books up so I can scan.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "which word is the name, and which words tell you what that name IS? The name goes inside the commas." Then do A together.
4. SCAN every book on the way past. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> mark B together, then re-check.
TRAP: putting commas around the whole sentence. Fix: point at the noun, take only the renaming words, student rewrites.
EXTENSION: Rewrite A so the appositive comes first and Bluey becomes the noun, then repunctuate the whole sentence.
HELP: Give students the two appositives Bluey and Ms Okafor; they box each one before adding commas.

you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - Exit ticket
you_do.check_rule: Tick each correct sentence. Fix any that is missing a comma.
check_items: A) The kelpie, Bluey, rounded up the sheep.
Bluey renames kelpie, so two commas hold the name in.
B) Our principal, Ms Okafor, opened the fair.
Cover Ms Okafor and the sentence still works.
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: name them inside commas.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A - commas around Bluey. B - commas around Ms Okafor.
1. MODEL: "In A the naming word is kelpie. Bluey tells us which kelpie, so a comma opens the name and a comma closes it."
2. SAY: "Now tick each sentence that matches. Fix any sentence that is missing a comma."
3. ASK: "Would A still be correct with no commas at all?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: no - the reader would run the name straight into the sentence.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> collect the books. Less -> rewrite B together, then collect.
5. SAY: "Next time you write about a person or a place your reader may not know, add commas and a few words that say who or what it is."
TRAP: ticking a sentence with only the opening comma. Fix: count the commas, then correct it.
